mainTopic: Carcass loss and hauling in damages, appraisal (שומא) for thieves and borrowers, and counting from a שליא that came out over two days
overview: The amud begins by finishing a ברייתא about a שומר whose animal was mauled. The תנא קמא says he brings witnesses, and אבא שאול says he brings the carcass to בית דין. The גמרא first suggests that they argue about פחת נבילה, the loss when the carcass drops in value. It then concludes that everyone agrees the ניזק bears that loss, and the argument is only about טורח נבילה, the work of hauling the carcass. אביי and רבא then define when that work rule matters: only when lifting the carcass out does not raise its value, like a beam that costs the same in town and in the field. Next, שמואל rules that the court appraises damaged items for נזקין but not for a גנב or a גזלן. The גמרא works out that a שואל does get appraisal, and it rules that way in the final הלכה. Finally, עולא rules on a שליא that came out over two days, and רבא objects that counting from the first day is a strictness that leads to a leniency. The גמרא then asks what עולא's ruling adds beyond a משנה, and its answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Witnesses or the carcass: the end of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא concludes. The תנא קמא says the שומר brings witnesses that the animal was mauled by אונס and he is exempt. אבא שאול says he brings the carcass to בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should bring witnesses that the animal was mauled through something out of his control, and he is exempt. אבא שאול says: he should bring the carcass to court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא about a שומר whose animal was killed by a wild beast. Two opinions explain what he must 'bring' to court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא reads the word 'עד' in the פסוק as 'witness', so the שומר proves it was an אונס and goes free. אבא שאול reads it as 'עדודה', the carcass, which he must bring to בית דין right away. This argument sets up the גמרא's next move.

keyTerms.meaning: Something beyond a person's control, like an attack by a wild animal
It was mauled or torn by a predator
The carcass. אבא שאול's reading of the word 'עד'
Exempt from paying

phrases.english: He should bring witnesses that it was mauled by circumstances beyond his control, and he is exempt.
Abba Shaul says:
He should bring the carcass to the court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ברייתא the גמרא began quoting before this section, as a possible source for who bears פחת נבילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: the שומר brings witnesses of the אונס and is exempt. אבא שאול: he brings the carcass to בית דין.

steps.title: Suggesting they argue about the carcass losing value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that אבא שאול and the תנא קמא argue about פחת נבילה. One holds the ניזק bears the drop in value, and the other holds the מזיק bears it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What, isn't this what they argue about? One Sage holds the loss in the carcass's value belongs to the damaged party, and the other holds it belongs to the one who caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to use the ברייתא to answer its question. It suggests the two opinions are really an argument about who loses when the carcass drops in value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ניזק bears the loss, the carcass must be valued right away so the payment is calculated correctly. That would explain why אבא שאול wants it brought to court. If the מזיק bears the loss, there is no rush, and witnesses are enough.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What, isn't it...?' A way of offering an explanation as a proof
They argue
The drop in value of the carcass
The damaged party
The one responsible for the damage

phrases.english: What, is it not about this that they disagree?

phrases.aramaic: דְּמָר סָבַר: פְּחַת נְבֵילָה דְּנִיזָּק הָוֵי,
phrases.english: That one Sage holds: the drop in the carcass's value is the damaged party's,
phrases.notes: 'One Sage' here is אבא שאול, which is why he wants the carcass brought for a quick valuation.

phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: it is the damager's?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reads the argument in the ברייתא as a proof about פחת נבילה.
steps.raayaObject: Who bears פחת נבילה: the ניזק or the מזיק
steps.raayaSupportSource: The argument between the תנא קמא and אבא שאול in the ברייתא

steps.title: No, they argue about the effort of hauling the carcass
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Everyone agrees the ניזק bears פחת נבילה. The argument is only about טורח נבילה, who must do the work of bringing the carcass.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees the loss is the damaged party's. Here they argue about the effort of handling the carcass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It says both Sages agree about the loss in value, and their real argument is about something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, the dispute is not about money lost but about work: who has to haul the carcass up and bring it to court. So the ברייתא cannot settle the question of פחת נבילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
The effort or trouble of handling and moving the carcass

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up פחת (the loss of value) with טורח (the work of moving it). The גמרא now says everyone agrees about פחת, and the argument is only about טורח.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees it is the damaged party's,
and here they disagree about the effort of the carcass;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 2 by moving the argument to a different issue.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the use of the ברייתא as a proof about פחת נבילה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument can be explained as being about טורח נבילה, not about who bears the loss in value.

steps.title: Support: אחרים say the pit owner must raise the ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which אחרים learn from 'כסף ישיב לבעליו והמת' that the owner of the בור must lift the ox out of his pit. This shows there really is a dispute about טורח נבילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was taught: Others say: How do we know the pit owner must bring the ox up out of his pit? The verse says: 'He shall restore money to its owner, and the dead animal.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its new reading by quoting a ברייתא. In it, a group called אחרים say the מזיק has to do the work of getting the carcass out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אחרים read 'and the dead animal' as something the pit owner must 'restore': he must bring the carcass back to its owner. Because the opinion is introduced as 'others say', it implies there is another view. That shows טורח נבילה is a real point of argument.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it was taught': brings a ברייתא as support
'Others say': a תנא quoted under this title
The owner of the pit
'The verse teaches': introduces a פסוק as the source

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא's final reading is that everyone agrees the ניזק bears פחת נבילה. The argument in the ברייתא is about טורח נבילה, and the opinion of אחרים shows such an argument exists.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the effort of retrieving a carcass is its own legal question, separate from who bears the loss in value.

phrases.english: And so it is taught: Others say:
From where do we know that it is upon the owner of the pit
to raise the ox from his pit?
The verse states:
"He shall restore money to its owner, and the dead animal."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the דחיה of step 3 by showing that an argument about טורח נבילה exists among the תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: That there is a תנאים dispute about who bears טורח נבילה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of אחרים reading 'כסף ישיב לבעליו והמת' (שמות 21:34)

steps.title: אביי asks what case the work of lifting the carcass is talking about
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבא to define the case of טורח נבילה. He shows that the obvious case does not work, because there the מזיק would lift the carcass out on his own anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: This 'effort of the carcass', what case is it? If you say that inside the pit the carcass is worth one זוז and at the edge it is worth four, then when he works to lift it out, he is working for his own benefit!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks רבא to explain when the rule of טורח נבילה would actually matter. He knocks down the most obvious case right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From Step 3, the ניזק keeps the carcass as part of his payment, and the מזיק pays the rest. So if lifting the carcass raises its value from one זוז to four, the מזיק pays three זוזים less. Then he would happily do the work by himself, and there is no need for a פסוק to force him.

keyTerms.meaning: The work of handling the carcass, here meaning lifting it out of the pit
What are the circumstances? What case is this?
If you say: introduces a suggested case that is about to be rejected
At the edge of the pit
He is working for his own benefit

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the higher carcass value helps the ניזק here. The ניזק gets full value either way. A more valuable carcass just means the מזיק has to add less money.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rava:
This 'effort of the carcass': what is the case?
phrases.notes: This is the duty to lift the dead ox out of the pit, from Step 4.

phrases.english: If you say that inside the pit it is worth one zuz,
and at the edge of the pit it is worth four;
then when he works, he is working for his own sake!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 4 proved that a view requiring טורח נבילה exists. Now אביי asks in what case that rule could have any effect.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what case would the Torah need to require the מזיק to lift the carcass out, if in the obvious case he gains by doing it himself?

steps.title: רבא: the rule is needed when the carcass is worth the same everywhere
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that טורח נבילה matters where the carcass is worth one זוז in the pit and also one זוז at the edge. Then the מזיק gains nothing from lifting it, so the Torah has to require it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: No, the rule is needed where inside the pit it is worth one זוז, and at the edge it is also worth one זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a case where the rule makes a real difference: lifting the carcass does not raise its value at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the price stays the same, the מזיק pays the same amount whether or not he lifts the carcass. He has no reason to bother. So the חידוש of טורח נבילה is that he must still do the work for the ניזק.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for... (introduces the case where the rule really matters)
Also
A זוז, a coin

phrases.english: He said to him: No, it is needed
where inside the pit it is worth one zuz,
and at the edge it is also worth one zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from Step 5 by giving a different case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule of טורח נבילה applies where the carcass's value does not change when it is lifted out, so the מזיק would have no reason of his own to lift it.

steps.title: Is there really a case where the price stays the same?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether it is realistic that a carcass would be worth the same in the pit and out of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is there such a case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions whether רבא's case ever really happens. This sets up the next step, which answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems obvious that something easy to reach is worth more than something stuck at the bottom of a pit. If רבא's case never happens, his answer would be useless.

keyTerms.meaning: But is there...? (doubts that something exists)
Like this, a case of this kind

phrases.english: But is there really a case like this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether רבא's case from Step 6 is realistic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does an item ever keep the same price whether it is hard or easy to reach?

steps.title: Yes: a beam costs the same in town and in the field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes and quotes a popular saying. A wooden beam sells for a זוז in town and also for a זוז out in the field, even though it still needs to be carried.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, for people say: A beam in the town for a זוז, a beam in the field for a זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves from everyday life that location does not always change the price, so רבא's case is real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A beam in the field still has to be hauled to town, yet people pay the same price for it. In the same way, a carcass can be worth the same in the pit and at its edge. So רבא's case stands, and טורח נבילה has a real case where it applies.

keyTerms.meaning: People say: a popular saying used as proof
A wooden beam
Town, city
Field, open country

steps.whatToRemember: טורח נבילה (the מזיק must lift the carcass out) only matters where lifting it does not raise its value. Otherwise the מזיק would do it anyway to lower what he pays. Such cases are real, like a beam that costs the same in town and in the field.
steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes defining the dispute from Step 3. Everyone agrees the ניזק bears פחת נבילה. The argument is only about who must do the work, and that matters only when the work does not change the price.

phrases.english: Yes, for people say:
A beam in the town sells for a zuz,
and a beam in the field sells for a zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the doubt from Step 7 and so supports רבא's case from Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. A popular saying shows that prices often do not change with location (a beam costs a זוז in town and in the field), so a carcass can be worth the same in the pit and at its edge.

steps.title: שמואל: appraisal is only for damages, and also for a borrower
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that the court does not do שומא for a גנב or גזלן, only for נזקין. He adds 'אף לשואל' and says that אבא (רב) agrees with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says: The court does not appraise for a thief or for a robber, only for damages. And I say: even for a borrower. And Abba agrees with me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ruling of שמואל about when the court appraises a damaged item or a dead animal. He ends with a short, unclear addition about a borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'שמין' means the court values the damaged item or carcass, gives it back to the owner, and the payer only covers the loss in value. For a thief or robber there is no appraisal: he keeps the damaged item and pays its full original value. The words 'אף לשואל' are short and unclear, and that sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The court appraises (sets a value on) the damaged item or carcass
A thief who steals secretly
A robber who takes openly by force
Damages (one person's property harming another's)
A borrower
Here, the name of רב, שמואל's colleague and teacher

phrases.english: Shmuel says:
They do not appraise, not for a thief
phrases.notes: The court doesn't value the damaged item and hand it back. The thief keeps it and pays its full original value.

phrases.english: and not for a robber,
but only for damages.
And I say: even for a borrower.
And Abba agrees with me.
phrases.notes: 'אבא' is רב, whose actual name was אבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין שָׁמִין לֹא לְגַנָּב וְלֹא לְגַזְלָן, אֶלָּא לְנִזָּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement about שומא. It connects to the earlier idea that the court appraises for נזקין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No appraisal for a גנב or גזלן, only for נזקין. 'Even for a borrower' is added, with רב agreeing.

steps.title: What did שמואל mean by 'even for a borrower'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which half of the ruling 'אף לשואל' belongs to. It could mean the court also appraises for a borrower, or that it also does not appraise for a borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Is he saying, 'Even for a borrower they appraise, and Abba agrees with me'? Or perhaps he is saying, 'And I say: even for a borrower they do not appraise, and Abba agrees with me'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about how to read שמואל's short addition. It sets up a search for a proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל gave two rules: 'no appraisal' for a thief or robber, and 'appraisal' for damages. 'Even for a borrower' could attach to either rule. The question is whether a borrower who damaged the item gets treated gently like a מזיק, or strictly like a thief.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (the גמרא then looks for a proof to settle it)
This is what he means
Or perhaps

steps.confusionAlert: Both readings use the same words 'וְאַבָּא מוֹדֶה לִי'. The only difference is whether the borrower gets 'שָׁמִין' or 'אֵין שָׁמִין'.

phrases.english: A question was asked to them:
Is this what he is saying:
even for a borrower they appraise,
and Abba agrees with me;
or perhaps, this is what he is saying:
And I say:
even for a borrower they do not appraise,
and Abba agrees with me?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to read the unclear ending of שמואל's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'אף לשואל' mean the court appraises for a borrower, or that it does not?

steps.title: Proof from the broken ax: no appraisal
steps.stepSummary: A man borrowed an ax and broke it. רב told him to pay for a whole, good ax. The גמרא concludes that there is no appraisal for a borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A certain man borrowed an ax from his friend and broke it. He came before רב. רב said to him: Go pay him a good ax. Learn from this: they do not appraise!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about רב to answer the question. Since שמואל said רב agrees with him, רב's ruling should show what שמואל meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court appraised, the broken ax would go back to the owner and the borrower would pay only the lost value. Instead, רב made him pay a full good ax. That looks like 'אֵין שָׁמִין' for a borrower.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a source is brought as a proof)
An ax
Good, whole, of full quality
Learn from it (a conclusion is drawn)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
that a certain man
who borrowed an ax from his friend
broke it.
He came before Rav.
He said to him:
Go pay him with a good ax.
Learn from it: they do not appraise!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דִּשְׁאֵיל נַרְגָּא מֵחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 10 from a real ruling of רב.
steps.raayaObject: The second reading: 'אף לשואל אין שמין'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the borrowed ax, where רב required payment of a full good ax.

steps.title: On the contrary: רב's silence shows they do appraise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the proof around. רב כהנא and רב אסי asked רב, 'Is this the law?!' and רב was silent. This shows he accepted their objection, so 'שָׁמִין' for a borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב: 'Is this the law?!' and he was silent. Learn from this: they appraise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from the ax story. It uses the same story to show the opposite conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's students protested the ruling of a full new ax. רב did not answer them, which means he agreed his ruling was wrong. So the story actually supports the first reading: the court appraises for a borrower, the way it does for נזקין.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary (the proof is flipped to show the opposite)
Is this the law? (a protest against a ruling)
He was silent (here, a sign of agreement)

steps.whatToRemember: The ax story first seems to show 'no appraisal for a borrower.' Because רב was silent when his students protested, the גמרא concludes the opposite: the court does appraise for a borrower.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רב's silence as ignoring the question. In the גמרא, staying silent after a challenge means he accepted it.

phrases.english: On the contrary,
from the fact that they said to him
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, to Rav:
"Is this the law?!"
and he was silent,
learn from it: they appraise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, מִדְּאָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 11's proof and flips the same story to the opposite conclusion.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection of the inference 'אֵין שָׁמִין' from the ax story.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof ignored the end of the story: רב's students challenged him and he stayed silent, which shows he took back his ruling.

steps.title: עולא and רב פפי argue about appraisal for a thief and a robber
steps.stepSummary: עולא, quoting רבי אלעזר, says the court does שומא for a גנב and a גזלן. רב פפי says it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: עולא said in the name of רבי אלעזר: The court appraises for a thief and for a robber. רב פפי said: It does not appraise for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument between אמוראים about the same question שמואל ruled on. Can a גנב or גזלן return the damaged item and pay only for the loss?
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said there is no שומא for a גנב or a גזלן. Now we see that this was argued: רבי אלעזר, through עולא, says there is שומא for them. רב פפי agrees with שמואל that there is not.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated, introducing an argument between אמוראים
A thief who steals secretly
A robber who takes openly by force
The court appraises: he returns the damaged item and pays for the loss in value

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר, אָמַר עוּלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: It was stated: עולא said that רבי אלעזר said:
The court appraises for a thief and for a robber.
רב פפי said: The court does not appraise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר, אָמַר עוּלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling that there is שומא for a שואל, the גמרא shows that the rule for a גנב and a גזלן is itself argued.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר: there is שומא for a גנב and a גזלן. רב פפי: there is no שומא for them.

steps.title: The final halacha: no appraisal for a thief or robber, but yes for a borrower
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that there is no שומא for a גנב or a גזלן, but there is שומא for a שואל, following רב כהנא and רב אסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: The court does not appraise for a thief or for a robber, but it does appraise for a borrower, following רב כהנא and רב אסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling for all three cases. It ties the borrower ruling back to the story of the broken ax.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a גנב and a גזלן, the הלכה follows רב פפי and שמואל: there is no שומא, so he must pay as if the item were whole. For a שואל there is שומא. This follows the objection of רב כהנא and רב אסי, which רב accepted by staying silent in Step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: And the final הלכה is
A borrower
Following the view of רב כהנא and רב אסי

steps.whatToRemember: Final הלכה: there is no שומא for a גנב or a גזלן, but there is שומא for a שואל.
steps.whyThisMatters: This settles the practical law. A thief or robber cannot hand back a damaged item and pay only for the loss, but a borrower can.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: the court does not appraise
neither for a thief nor for a robber,
but for a borrower, the court appraises,
following רב כהנא and רב אסי.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא: אֵין שָׁמִין לֹא לְגַנָּב וְלֹא לְגַזְלָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument from Step 13 and confirms the borrower ruling from Step 12.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: No שומא for a גנב or a גזלן. There is שומא for a שואל, as רב כהנא and רב אסי said.

steps.title: Counting from the first day when an afterbirth comes out over two days
steps.stepSummary: עולא, quoting רבי אלעזר, rules that if a שליא came out partly on one day and partly on the next, we count her days from the first day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And עולא said in the name of רבי אלעזר: An afterbirth that came out partly on the first day and partly on the second day, we count for her from the first day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: another ruling of עולא in the name of רבי אלעזר. It is about a woman who delivers a שליא, which makes her טמאה like after a birth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her days of טומאה are counted from the birth. Here the שליא came out over two days, so it is unclear which day counts as the birth. עולא says to start counting from the first day.

keyTerms.meaning: Afterbirth. A woman who delivers it is treated as having given birth
Part of it
We count the days

phrases.english: And עולא said that רבי אלעזר said:
An afterbirth that came out partly on the first day
and partly on the second day,
we count for her from the first day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, linked to Step 13 only because it is another ruling of עולא in the name of רבי אלעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a שליא comes out over two days, the count begins from the first day.

steps.title: רבא objects: a strictness that leads to a leniency
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether עולא counts from the first day to be strict. He points out that this also makes her טהורה earlier, which is a קולא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: What is your thinking, to be strict?! It is a strictness that leads to a leniency, because you make her pure counting from the first day!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges עולא's ruling. He shows that the 'strict' approach backfires.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Counting from day one is strict because it makes her טמאה from the first day. But the end of her period of טומאה is counted from that same day, so she also becomes טהורה a day earlier. If the birth really happened on the second day, she would be treated as טהורה while still טמאה. So this is a חומרא דאתי לידי קולא.

keyTerms.meaning: What is your thinking?
To be strict
A strictness that leads to a leniency
You make her טהורה (pure)

steps.confusionAlert: Counting from the first day is not only strict. The same starting day also sets when her טומאה ends, so it makes her טהורה a day early. That early end is the problem רבא is pointing to.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: מָה דַעְתָּךְ, לְחוּמְרָא?!
phrases.english: רבא said to him: What is your thinking? To be strict?!
It is a strictness that leads to a leniency,
because you make her pure by counting from the first day!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: מָה דַעְתָּךְ, לְחוּמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning behind עולא's ruling in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's ruling to count from the first day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The only reason to count from day one is to be strict. But the same count makes her טהורה earlier, so the strictness ends up producing a forbidden leniency.

steps.title: רבא's own approach: be strict, but count from the second day
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the woman is careful and treats herself as possibly impure from the first day, but she counts her days only from the second day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: when it comes to being careful, she is careful starting from the first day. But when it comes to counting her days, she counts only from the second day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא drops the idea that we simply count from the first day, and gives his own ruling that is strict in both directions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 16, רבא showed that counting from the first day makes her טהורה a day earlier, which is a קולא. So now he splits it: she worries about טומאה from day one, but her count does not start until day two. This way she never ends up טהורה too early.

keyTerms.meaning: To be concerned / to be careful about a possibility
She is concerned (she acts strictly)
To count (the days)
From the second (day)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the birth happened on the second day. He is saying we are strict both ways: she worries about טומאה from day one, but she starts counting from day two.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
To be concerned — she is concerned;
But to count — she does not count
phrases.notes: Some versions have the extra letter in round brackets and some don't. Either way it means "count."

phrases.english: except from the second day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After raising the problem in step 16, רבא offers his own ruling to avoid the קולא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Regarding concern, she is strict from the first day. Regarding counting, she counts only from the second day.

steps.title: What does עולא's ruling add? A משנה already teaches it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what עולא's ruling teaches. If it teaches that part of a שליא always comes with a baby, a משנה already says that.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is עולא teaching us? That part of a שליא never comes out without a baby? We already learned this in a משנה: if part of a שליא came out, it is forbidden to eat, because a שליא is a sign of a baby in a woman and a sign of a baby in an animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges עולא's ruling by saying it seems to repeat something an existing משנה already teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's ruling assumes the birth began when the שליא began coming out. That means a שליא is treated as containing a baby. The משנה in חולין already says this, since it calls a שליא a sign of a baby. So why did עולא need to say it?

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (asks what a ruling adds)
Afterbirth / placenta
Baby / fetus
We already learned (in a משנה)
A sign

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
phrases.notes: "He" is עולא, whose ruling we saw in step 15.

phrases.english: That there is no part of an afterbirth without a fetus?
We already learned it:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in חולין 77a, about slaughtering a pregnant animal.

phrases.english: An afterbirth, part of which came out,
is forbidden to eat;
it is a sign of a fetus in a woman,
and a sign of a fetus in an animal!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how to count the days to asking why עולא's ruling was needed at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's ruling that we count from the first day when the שליא came out over two days
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The idea behind the ruling, that a שליא always has a baby with it, is already stated in a משנה, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Beginning the answer: from the משנה alone we might have thought differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to answer: if we only had the משנה, we might have understood it another way.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we had only the משנה, I would have said...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its answer. It starts to explain what we might have wrongly concluded from the משנה alone, and the answer continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a standard defense: a later ruling is needed because the earlier source could have been read differently. The actual reading the גמרא has in mind is not stated yet, so we have to wait for the continuation.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה (the source just quoted)
I would have said (what we might have wrongly thought)

phrases.english: If I knew it only from the Mishnah,
I would have said...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the challenge from step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The earlier source alone could have been misread, so the later ruling is still needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Not yet stated on this amud. It continues on the next amud.
